```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%", raster3d = 1e5, dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

ggplot3d adds three-dimensional layers and a z position scale to [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/), the R package for building plots from data and aesthetic mappings. This tutorial assumes basic R and data frames. It ends with a surface, observations and a saved plot.

1. **Map** positions with `aes()`.

2. **Draw** a surface with `geom_surface_3d()`.

3. **Save** the plot with `ggsave()`.

## Installation

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/ggplot3d")
```

Source installation needs a C++17 compiler. The [README installation section](https://github.com/gcol33/ggplot3d#installation) lists the tools for each operating system.

## Plotting observations

Each row records three positions in arbitrary units. Map the column names to x, y and z. The call returns a ggplot object that can be printed, extended and saved.

```{r points, fig.alt="Three observations positioned along x, y and z axes."}
observations <- data.frame(id = c("a", "b", "c"),
  east = c(-1, 0, 1), north = c(0, 1, -1), height = c(0.4, 1.2, 0.8))
p <- ggplot(observations, aes(east, north, z = height)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = PAL["red"]) + coord_3d()
p
```

The z axis labels the height column. The camera projects these three positions onto the plotting page. Change its angles in [Camera and framing](camera.html).

## Adding a surface

The surface data contain one row for every pair of grid positions. Its heights describe a curved surface in the same units as the observations. Both layers contribute geometry to the panel scene, the collection used to resolve which parts are visible.

```{r surface, fig.alt="A blue curved surface with three red observations at different heights."}
surface <- expand.grid(east = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 12),
                       north = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 12))
surface$height <- with(surface, exp(-(east^2 + north^2)))
p <- ggplot(surface, aes(east, north, z = height)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_point_3d(data = observations, size = 3, colour = PAL["red"]) +
  coord_3d()
p
```

Grid neighbours form triangles. Surface pieces cover observations wherever they lie in front of them. [Layers](layers.html) also shows columns, contours, meshes and statistical surfaces.

## Reading another table

For a file with other column names, change the file path and the names inside the mapping. This example writes a temporary comma-separated file so the whole example can run in a fresh session.

```{r read-table, fig.alt="Three observations read from a comma-separated file and mapped to the east, north and height axes."}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(observations, path, row.names = FALSE)
measured <- read.csv(path)
ggplot(measured, aes(east, north, z = height)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3) + coord_3d()
unlink(path)
```

## Supplying a surface height

A surface needs a z mapping. The following call shows the message produced by a missing mapping.

```{r missing-z}
tryCatch(
  print(ggplot(surface, aes(east, north)) + geom_surface_3d() + coord_3d()),
  error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e)))
```

Map the height column to z to connect the grid points.

```{r corrected, fig.alt="A blue curved surface after supplying its height mapping."}
ggplot(surface, aes(east, north, z = height)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d()
```

## Saving the plot

The default backend draws vector geometry. The file extension selects the graphics device. Use the raster backend for a scene rendered into pixels; [Output backends](backends.html) explains resolution and device requirements.

```{r save}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".pdf")
ggsave(path, p, width = 5, height = 4.5)
file.info(path)$size > 0
unlink(path)
```
